title: Acute Onset Esotropia: A Clinical Masterclass
summary: Acute onset esotropia (AOE) in children or adults is a potential neuro-ophthalmic emergency. While often benign and idiopathic, it requires a rigorous diagnostic algorithm to exclude life-threatening intracranial pathology such as tumors, hydrocephalus, or Chiari malformations.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Acute Onset Esotropia (AOE) is defined as a sudden, manifest inward deviation of the eyes in a previously orthotropic individual (or one with stable microtropia). Unlike congenital esotropia, AOE presents with symptomatic diplopia and often maintains high potential for stereopsis if treated promptly. It spans a spectrum from benign decompensated phoria to high-acuity neurological presentations involving the brainstem or cerebellum.

rows: Occurs after monocular occlusion (e.g., patching) or sudden vision loss.
Relatively large angle, minimal hyperopia, sudden onset without obvious trigger.
Associated with uncorrected myopia or excessive near-work; distance ET > near ET.

sections.title: MANDATORY RED FLAGS (IMAGING NEEDED)
content: Papilledema or Blurred Disc Margins on Fundoscopy
Incomitance (Deviation varies with gaze direction)
Abduction Deficits (Pseudo-6th Nerve Palsy)
Systemic Neurological Signs (Ataxia, Dysmetria, Hyperreflexia)
Severe Morning Headache or Projectile Vomiting
Torticollis (New onset compensatory head tilt)
Nystagmus (Especially downbeat or gaze-evoked)

sections.title: The Essential Sensorimotor Workup
content: Cycloplegic Refraction: Use 1% Atropine or Cyclopentolate to find latent hyperopia.
Prism Cover Test (PCT): Measure at 1/3m and 6m; check all 9 cardinal positions.
Stereopsis Testing: Titmus or Randot to assess binocular potential.
Duction/Version: Check for subtle abduction limitation (CN VI).
Worth 4-Dot Test: Assess for suppression vs. diplopia.
Near Point of Convergence (NPC): Evaluate accommodative effort.

rows: Age-related, LR/SR pulley displacement, small vertical.
Distance ET much greater than near ET.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Observations
content: Chiari I Malformation: Classically associated with AOE and downbeat nystagmus.
Cycloplegic Refraction is non-negotiable; AOE can be a high-AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia presenting late.
Type II (Franceschetti) usually has high stereopsis potential with surgery.
If the ET is incomitant, it is NEVER idiopathic until CNS lesions are ruled out.
Heavy Eye Syndrome: High myopia causing LR-SR band displacement, mimicking AOE.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Full Cycloplegic Refraction. Prescribe full plus power found.
Step 2: Neurological Screening. If red flags or incomitance, order MRI Brain/Orbits with contrast.
Step 3: Prism Adaptation. Use Fresnel prisms to neutralize diplopia and assess for 'eating the prism'.
Step 4: Botulinum Toxin. Consider for small angles or as a diagnostic tool for binocularity.
Step 5: Surgical Intervention. Usually Bilateral Medial Rectus (BMR) recession based on the largest measured angle.

content.explanation: S: Sudden onset; T: Tumors/Tension (ICP); O: Optical (Refractive); R: Restricted (Mechanical); M: Myasthenia/Muscle.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Neuroimaging Criteria
sections.content: Recent studies (e.g., Lion et al.) emphasize that while the incidence of brain tumors in isolated AOE is low (<5%), the presence of even subtle incomitance or failure to resolve with correction increases the risk of CNS pathology significantly. Modern high-resolution MRI with 'FIESTA' or 'CISS' sequences is preferred to visualize the CN VI cistern portion and the posterior fossa/craniocervical junction.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Amblyopia Risk: Significant in children under age 7.
Loss of Stereopsis: Irreversible if duration of misalignment is prolonged (>6 months).
Overcorrection: A risk of consecutive exotropia if surgery is too aggressive.
Recurrence: High in Type III Bielschowsky if myopia and near-strain are not managed.

sections.title: Special Population: Sagging Eye Syndrome
content: Affects elderly patients (involutional).
Degeneration of the LR-SR intermuscular band.
Leads to sagging of the Lateral Rectus muscle pulley.
Presents as a small-angle esotropia and a 'cyclovertical' deviation (hypertropia).
Diagnosis confirmed via thin-cut coronal MRI showing muscle displacement.
